clue.text: Where broth may be black bird of prey

blocks.note: b is the black of a pencil, the letter stamped on the side of a 2B
an owl hunts live prey through the night

explanation.surface: Soup sitting in the same sentence as a dark hunting bird.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Black bird of prey' wants to be one dark hunter, and the split falls between the colour and the bird. The pencil marking is where the one-letter convention for black comes from.
explanation.definitionFit: Broth is served in a bowl, so the definition names the vessel by what is poured into it rather than by a synonym.

clue.text: Period of small misfortunes - like losing to a tortoise, reports suggest

indicators.note: A report is what somebody is heard to say, so what counts is the sound of the words and not the way they are spelt.

blocks.note: in Aesop's fable the hare loses the race to the tortoise, and that is not his finest day

explanation.surface: An animal humiliated in a race by a tortoise.
explanation.walkthrough: The fable does the work: only one animal is famous for losing a race to a tortoise, and English pronounces that animal exactly like the stuff on your head.
explanation.definitionFit: A bad hair day is the day when nothing quite goes right — a run of small irritations rather than one disaster.

clue.text: Baked pie? Good, now what's in it?

definitions.note: The definition is put as a question — what is inside the pie — rather than as a noun, which is how the setter makes the filling double as the clue's punchline.

indicators.note: What comes out of an oven is never laid out the way it went in, so the letters beside it are taken in a new order.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, ten letters, question mark and comma ignored

explanation.surface: Asking what filling went into a pie fresh from the oven.
explanation.walkthrough: Everything before the last question mark reads as appreciation of the cooking and is the raw material; the question itself is the definition. Game pie is a real dish, so surface and answer share a kitchen.
explanation.definitionFit: A wood pigeon is standard game-pie filling in Britain, so it answers the question of what is inside one.

clue.text: What makes you die of cold?

definitions.text: What makes you die of cold?

blocks.note: the reading the surface pushes: perishing from exposure

blocks.clueFragment: What makes you die of cold?
blocks.note: the reading the setter means: a die is the singular of dice, a small cube, and this one is made of frozen water

explanation.surface: A question about what could freeze a person to death.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Die' is the singular of 'dice', a small cube, and once it is read as a noun the question stops being about hypothermia and starts being about what turns out cubes of cold by the tray.
explanation.definitionFit: An appliance exists to churn out those cubes, so the whole question — what makes you a die of cold — is answered by naming it.

clue.text: Business trouble

blocks.note: read as a noun: a firm, an enterprise, a going one
read as a verb: to worry somebody, to give them cause for disquiet

explanation.surface: A firm running into difficulties.
explanation.walkthrough: Two words and two definitions, with the join invisible because the pair also make a plausible phrase. One half is a noun and the other a verb, and the answer serves as both.
explanation.definitionFit: A concern is a business — a going concern — and to concern somebody is to trouble them, the noun and the verb of one word.

clue.text: Resents '80s film's outlook on life

blocks.note: to mind a thing is to object to it — 'I don't mind' is granting permission
Spielberg's E.T. reached cinemas in 1982

explanation.surface: Somebody still smarting about a film from the eighties.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Resents' has to be read as a third-person verb — he minds it — which is what puts an s in the middle of the answer. The film is the one with the flying bicycle.
explanation.definitionFit: A mindset is the settled way somebody takes things, an established outlook on life rather than a passing mood.

clue.text: Rise and criticise church? That's just retribution

blocks.note: to come up is to rise — the sun comes up
to pan a show is to review it savagely
the Church of England, the established church, is shortened to its two initials

explanation.surface: A congregation told to stand up and find fault with their own church.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark is where the surface gives up, because no church asks that of its members. 'Pan' is the reviewer's word for a savaging, and a church in a clue is almost always the English one in two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A comeuppance is the punishment somebody has had coming to them, so the retribution is just by definition.

clue.text: 'I' - one that's Athenian, primarily?

indicators.note: Primarily means first of all, so each word in the run gives up nothing but the letter it begins with.

blocks.note: the opening letter of the quoted letter, which is the whole of it
the opening letter of the second word in the run
even the small joining word gives up its first letter
the opening letter of the last word, and the run is printed in clue order

explanation.surface: Someone checking whether the letter I counts as an Athenian one.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue spells its answer with the same words that describe it, which is what the question mark is owning. Everyman plants one of these first-letter clues in nearly every puzzle.
explanation.definitionFit: Read straight, the whole clue describes the thing: iota is the Greek alphabet's I, and Greek is what Athens speaks.

clue.text: At first, Everyman's dreary, vacuous, dreary - I'm going round in circles

indicators.note: At first asks for the opening letter of each word it governs and nothing beyond it.
A vacuous thing is empty in the middle, so the word keeps only the letters at its two ends.

blocks.note: the opening letter of the setter's own name
the opening letter of the word beside it, still under the same instruction
the same word over again, this time hollowed out to its first and last letters

explanation.surface: Everyman running himself down twice over and coming over giddy.
explanation.walkthrough: The setter is describing himself, which is the Everyman habit, and the repetition is not there for emphasis: the two identical words are worked on in two different ways.
explanation.definitionFit: An eddy is water turning in a small circle against the current, so going round in circles is both what it does and what it is.

clue.text: Condemn atmosphere that's reactionary

indicators.note: A reactionary wants things put back the way they were, so the word beside it is read back to front.

blocks.note: the mood of a room is its atmosphere

explanation.surface: A backward-looking atmosphere being denounced.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reactionary' is the political word doing a mechanical job, and it is the only instruction in the clue. The verb sense of the answer — to sentence somebody to a fate — is older than the gloomy noun everyone knows.
explanation.definitionFit: To doom somebody is to condemn them to a fate, the verb sense that survives in 'doomed to fail'.

clue.text: A grandma won at chess, did you say? Not so fast

indicators.note: Asking what somebody said points at the noise the words make, so the first part is written down as it is heard rather than as it is spelt.

blocks.note: nanny is a British child's word for a grandmother, and 'a nanny' run together is what the first five letters say aloud
checkmate ends the game, so the player who mates has won; these letters are spelt as they sound

explanation.surface: Someone double-checking a claim that grandma beat them at chess.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not so fast' is exactly what you say to somebody claiming a win, which is why it reads as part of the argument instead of as the definition. Only the first half of the wordplay changes its spelling.
explanation.definitionFit: An animated talker is lively and quick, so what is unanimated lacks that pace — sluggish, not the interruption the surface offers.

clue.text: If you're spoonfed, this may put words in your mouth

definitions.text: If you're spoonfed, this may put words in your mouth

blocks.clueFragment: may put words in your mouth
blocks.note: the reading the surface pushes: the idiom for claiming somebody said what they never said
the reading the setter means: what a spoon carries can include pasta moulded into letters, so words genuinely do arrive in your mouth

explanation.surface: Somebody being fed opinions they never expressed themselves.
explanation.walkthrough: The idiom is figurative everywhere except here, where the words are shapes floating in a bowl. 'Spoonfed' carries both senses too — told what to think, and fed a spoonful at a time.
explanation.definitionFit: Alphabet soup is sold with letter-shaped pasta in it, so a spoonful really can deliver words to the mouth of whoever is being fed.

clue.text: Titian to rub out credit

indicators.note: Something out is out of true and out of order, so the letters before it will not stay in the arrangement they are given.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, eleven letters

explanation.surface: Titian being told to erase a credit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rub out' is one phrase in the surface and two separate jobs in the wordplay, with the rubbing part of the material and the out doing the shuffling. Naming a painter is apt: the word belongs to the art world.
explanation.definitionFit: An attribution is the credit given to a work's maker, the label saying whose hand painted it.

clue.text: Swimming pool - mine - so refuse to share

indicators.note: Things that are swimming are adrift and no longer where they were put, so the letters beside it are rearranged.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, ten letters, the dashes ignored

explanation.surface: Somebody in the water announcing that the pool is theirs alone.
explanation.walkthrough: The dashes make 'mine' look like an aside rather than material, and that is the only thing hiding a very plain anagram. The surface even acts out the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To monopolise something is to keep the whole of it to yourself, which is refusing anybody else a turn.

clue.text: Dull, like a perfume you don't smell?

definitions.text: like a perfume you don't smell?

blocks.note: read straight: flat, without spark or imagination

blocks.clueFragment: like a perfume you don't smell?
blocks.note: read through the Latin: to inspire is to breathe in, so a scent never drawn up the nose has not been breathed in at all

explanation.surface: A perfume so faint that nobody ever notices it.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark is the setter owning the second reading, because no dictionary defines the word that way. Inspire, respire and expire all come from the same Latin verb for breathing.
explanation.definitionFit: Uninspired work is dull and unlit by any idea; and since inspire once meant to breathe in, a perfume left unsniffed is literally not inspired.

clue.text: Topless seaside town? Amen

indicators.note: Something topless has lost whatever sat on top of it, so the word goes without its opening letter.

blocks.note: Brighton is the big resort on the Sussex coast, and the B on the front of it is what a topless word loses

explanation.surface: A question about a resort that has gone without its top.
explanation.walkthrough: The joke in the surface is the beach, and the instruction is that a word can be topless too. 'Amen' and the answer are both ways of saying you agree with what has just been said.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying amen to something is endorsing it out loud, which is the approving shout the answer makes.

clue.text: Tea and slice of nougat gives you wind

indicators.note: A slice is cut from the end of what follows, and the end taken here is the front: one letter, not a chunk.

blocks.note: Typhoo is a British tea brand, on grocers' shelves since 1903
the letter cut off the front of the word

explanation.surface: Tea and a bit of confectionery leaving you with indigestion.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition sounds like the trapped sort of wind the surface is complaining about, and it is the meteorological sort. A tea in a clue is often a brand rather than a drink.
explanation.definitionFit: A typhoon is the Pacific name for a hurricane, so the definition covers it by the one thing it is made of.

clue.text: Put an end to slippery oil baths - no time!

indicators.note: Something slippery will not stay where it is put, so the letters beside it slide into another order.
No time means the time is not there, so the letter that stands for it drops out before anything else is done.

blocks.note: t is the standard short form for time, as in a physics formula
the seven letters of the phrase once that t has gone, taken as they stand before the shuffle

explanation.surface: A demand to scrap slippery oil baths when the clock is against you.
explanation.walkthrough: The exclamation mark sells 'no time!' as impatience, and it is an instruction to remove a letter. That letter has to go before the shuffle or the count comes out at eight.
explanation.definitionFit: To abolish a practice is to put an end to it for good, by decree rather than by neglect.

clue.text: Stink surrounding old, old, rough ruffian

indicators.note: What surrounds a thing closes round it on both sides, so these letters split and wrap the ones named next.
A rough job is one done with no care for order, so the letters beside it come out in a different arrangement.

blocks.note: a room that hums stinks, in the British slang sense of the verb
o is the standard short form of old, and the second old is written out in full

explanation.surface: A smelly old thug of the roughest kind.
explanation.walkthrough: Three adjectives in a row read as a description and are two separate instructions, one of them repeating the same word in two forms. The slang sense of a stink — that it hums — is worth banking.
explanation.definitionFit: A hoodlum is a violent petty criminal, the American word for the street thug that 'ruffian' names in older English.

clue.text: Was in charge of twerp somewhere in Burma

blocks.note: whoever ran the place was in charge of it
a goon is a thug or an idiot, depending on which way you use it

explanation.surface: Being put in charge of an idiot out in Burma.
explanation.walkthrough: Both halves are plain synonyms and the difficulty is all in the join, since 'in charge of twerp' reads as one job description. Rangoon is the old colonial spelling, renamed Yangon in 1989.
explanation.definitionFit: Rangoon is Burma's biggest city and its former capital, so the definition places it by country rather than naming it.

clue.text: Dealing with part of the eye, actual metal's inserted

definitions.text: Dealing with part of the eye

indicators.note: Something inserted is pushed into the middle of what is already there, so the longer word opens up to take the shorter one.

blocks.note: what is actual is real
tin is the metal a tin can is named after

explanation.surface: An eye operation in which actual metal goes in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Actual metal' reads as one phrase insisting the metal is genuine, and it is two words with two different jobs. A metal in a clue is usually one of the short ones.
explanation.definitionFit: Retinal is the adjective from retina, the light-sensitive layer at the back of the eye, so it deals with exactly that part of it.

clue.text: Not included: how crossword setter found anagram for 'pothole'?

indicators.note: The clue says the word outright: the letters named next are to be rearranged into something else.

blocks.note: the question asks where he got it from, and you make one word out of the letters of another
the seven letters of the quoted word in a new order

explanation.surface: A setter being asked where he found an anagram of a word for a hole in the road.
explanation.walkthrough: The colon reads as a heading introducing the question, and it is separating a definition from its wordplay. The setter is describing his own trade, which is how the question hides its answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Somebody out of the loop has been left off the circulation list, so the news goes round without ever reaching them.

clue.text: Volcano: pet name some ignored

indicators.note: Ignoring some of what is written means keeping the rest, and the rest wanted here is one unbroken run of letters.

blocks.note: four consecutive letters run through this phrase, starting one letter in and crossing the space

explanation.surface: A pet's name that some people took no notice of.
explanation.walkthrough: The colon after the definition makes the rest look like a list entry rather than an instruction, and 'ignored' is doing the hiding. Etna is the Sicilian giant, Europe's tallest active volcano.
explanation.definitionFit: Etna is the volcano above Catania in Sicily, erupting often enough to be the first one most people can name.

clue.text: Rejected plans to pester people online

indicators.note: What is rejected is thrown back, so the letters beside it are read back to front.

blocks.note: a map is a plan of a place, as in a street plan

explanation.surface: A scheme for annoying people on the internet being turned down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rejected plans' is such a natural pair that the first word looks like an adjective rather than an order. The answer is a verb here, so the definition has to be one too.
explanation.definitionFit: To spam is to fire unwanted messages at people by email or post, which is pestering them online.

clue.text: Celebrity in jumper maybe sending invoice

definitions.note: Celebrity is used in its abstract sense of star status rather than meaning a famous person, which is what lets an -ing phrase stand for it.

indicators.note: A jumper is one example of the thing wanted rather than the thing itself, so the word stands for the wider class it belongs to.

blocks.note: a jumper is one kind of top, the garment worn above the waist
billing a customer is sending them the invoice

explanation.surface: A famous face in a woolly jumper, posting the bills out.
explanation.walkthrough: The invoice sense and the poster sense of the second word are unrelated, and the clue only ever offers the accounting one. 'Maybe' is the standard signal that a word is an example, not a synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: Top billing is having your name first and largest on the poster, which is star status made visible.

clue.text: Pork pie purveyor admitted to Juilliard

indicators.note: Somebody admitted to a place has been let inside it, so the letters wanted are sitting within the word that follows.

blocks.note: four consecutive letters run through the name of the New York music conservatoire

explanation.surface: A pie seller who won a place at the Juilliard School.
explanation.walkthrough: Cockney rhyming slang shortens 'pork pies' to 'porkies' and uses them for lies, which is the whole of the definition. 'Admitted' pulls double duty: confessing on the surface, containing in the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: In Cockney rhyming slang a pork pie is a lie, so whoever deals in them is a liar.

clue.text: Mad monk? I'll supply drink

indicators.note: Read as the adverb of supple — done flexibly, with a bend in it — so the letters beside it give way into another order.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, ten letters, the contraction counted as it is spelt

explanation.surface: Rasputin offering to fetch the drinks.
explanation.walkthrough: The trap is reading 'supply drink' as one action, the monk fetching a round. Say the word as SUPP-ly, the adverb from supple, and it turns into the instruction instead. The mad monk of the surface is Rasputin.
explanation.definitionFit: Almond milk is the nut-based drink people pour into coffee in place of dairy, so 'drink' defines it by its class.

clue.text: Crossword setter getting commercial for booze

blocks.note: the setter writing the clue refers to himself as me
a commercial is an ad

explanation.surface: The setter of this puzzle taking an advertising deal and being paid in drink.
explanation.walkthrough: A crossword setter in a clue is almost always the two letters of the first person, and Everyman signs himself into his own puzzles more than most. Mead is the honey wine of Anglo-Saxon feasting halls.
explanation.definitionFit: Mead is fermented honey and water, an alcoholic drink of the oldest kind, which is all 'booze' asks for.
